headline: State desk: North Carolina weighs 400 stores; Alaska may double limits
dek: North Carolina's cannabis council meets 17 November, Massachusetts debates drive-throughs, Alaska weighs bigger concentrate limits and Utah sets $150 vouchers.
key_points: North Carolina's Advisory Council on Cannabis meets on 17 November to settle its final recommendations, including a model with about 400 private dispensaries fed by a state-run warehouse.
Massachusetts regulators discuss drive-through sales on 17 November, the same day a police survey found 92% of 161 officers want legal sales kept.
Alaska's Marijuana Control Board weighs two drafts on 18-19 November that would double the daily concentrate limit from 7 to 14 grams.
Utah proposed rules for $150-a-month medical cannabis vouchers for Medicaid and Medicare patients, with comments open to 15 December.
body: The week after the midterms has shifted the action back to state agencies. Four of them have decisions this week that could reshape how cannabis is sold: a legalization blueprint in North Carolina, drive-through windows in Massachusetts, purchase limits in Alaska and patient subsidies in Utah. In Florida, Trulieve keeps adding stores.
## North Carolina: a hybrid market on the table

North Carolina's Advisory Council on Cannabis, created by Gov. Josh Stein in June 2025, holds its full meeting on Tuesday 17 November from 1:30 to 5 p.m. at the health department's headquarters in Raleigh. The Marijuana Herald reported that the council plans to finish a draft report by 1 December, vote on it on 15 December and deliver recommendations to the governor by 31 December.

Minutes from the council's 23 October market subcommittee, as summarised by the Herald, describe three options. One is a hybrid in which the state runs warehousing and distribution while about 400 privately owned dispensaries sell to adults. The others are a state-run retail system modelled on North Carolina's alcohol (ABC) stores, and a fully private market. Members have not picked one, and the report is expected to set out the pros and cons of each. They did broadly agree on separate licences for cultivation, processing and retail rather than vertical integration, and on allowing low-dose THC drinks of about 5 to 10 mg in bars, wine shops and grocery stores.

The federal picture still weighs on the choice, especially the legal risk of state employees selling cannabis directly. As we reported on 15 November, an Oklahoma enforcement official told a council subcommittee to keep licences tight. Any market would need the General Assembly's approval when it meets in January, where Democrats will hold the House majority in 2027, according to NC Newsline.
> North Carolina is drafting its market from scratch, and the choice between 400 private stores and state-run shops will decide who can enter it.
## Massachusetts: drive-throughs and a police survey

The Massachusetts Cannabis Control Commission's 17 November agenda includes a discussion of drive-throughs at marijuana establishments, alongside its fall regulatory round and a study on regulating hemp-derived cannabinoids. The item is listed for discussion, not a vote, and the Herald noted the commission has not said how drive-through sales would be regulated.

Some stores already offer versions of it. Elysian in Quincy was offering window pickup for adult-use pre-orders by August, Talking Joints Memo reported, and Theory Wellness in Chicopee has served medical patients at a window since 2021. Capeway Cannabis in Bourne won approval from Bourne's Board of Health for a drive-through bay with six cameras, but still needs the commission's sign-off, CapeNews.net reported.

The commission also publicised a survey for the Law Enforcement Action Partnership in which 92% of 161 current and retired Massachusetts officers backed keeping licensed sales, 54% under current rules and 38% with changes. The online survey ran from 6 to 18 October and was not a random sample, the Herald noted. It follows voters' rejection of Question 8 earlier this month.
## Alaska: bigger purchase limits

Alaska's Marijuana Control Board meets on 18 and 19 November in Anchorage to consider two drafts that would raise daily purchase limits, the Herald reported from a 9 November staff memo. Today a store may sell one person up to one ounce of flower, 7 grams of concentrate or products with 5,600 mg of THC in a day.

Version one would raise the concentrate limit to 14 grams and the THC limit to 11,200 mg, and track purchases in units. Version two would set an equivalency in which one ounce of flower equals 14 grams of concentrate or 140 ten-milligram servings, which works out to 1,400 mg of THC in edibles. Both would let on-site consumption venues apply standard retail limits instead of today's one gram of flower or 25 mg edible. If the board approves a draft, it goes to the Department of Law and then out for public comment, so nothing changes immediately.
## Utah: $150 vouchers for patients on Medicaid or Medicare

Utah published proposed rules in the 15 November State Bulletin for a medical cannabis voucher programme created by Senate Bill 121. Patients with an active medical card who are enrolled in Medicaid or Medicare could get $150 a month, usable at any licensed medical cannabis pharmacy and also for delivery and state transaction fees, the Herald reported. A nonprofit would run the programme and could not own any cannabis business. Comments close on 15 December, and the rules could take effect on 22 December.

Funding is capped at up to $300,000 a year, according to the state's Center for Medical Cannabis. By MetaFlora's arithmetic, that pays a full year of vouchers for about 166 patients, so demand is likely to exceed the money.
## Florida: Trulieve's 172nd store
Trulieve opened a dispensary in Tampa on West Hillsborough Avenue, with a grand opening on 20 November. The Herald counts it as Trulieve's 172nd Florida location and 272nd overall.
## What to watch

17 November: North Carolina council meeting and the Massachusetts drive-through discussion. 18-19 November: Alaska's purchase-limit vote. 1 and 15 December: North Carolina's draft and final vote. 15 December: Utah comment deadline.
